clinicalPearls: Defined by progressive, unilateral palsy of several or all cranial nerves on one side without long-tract signs or raised intracranial pressure
The absence of motor and sensory long-tract signs and of papilloedema distinguishes it from an intra-axial brainstem lesion
It reflects a process at or around the skull base picking off cranial nerves sequentially as they exit their foramina
The commonest cause is an infiltrative skull-base malignancy such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma or other locally invasive tumour
Other causes include skull-base metastases, lymphoma, chordoma, meningioma and, less often, granulomatous or infective basal disease
Careful documentation of which cranial nerves are involved helps localise the lesion within the skull base
Management is generic and directed at the underlying cause, guided by skull-base imaging and biopsy or nasopharyngeal assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Garcin syndrome arises when a pathological process at the base of the skull progressively involves the cranial nerves as they traverse or exit their bony foramina on one side. Most often this is an infiltrative or compressive skull-base malignancy, classically nasopharyngeal carcinoma extending through the skull base, which sequentially compresses or infiltrates multiple cranial nerves. Because the lesion lies extra-axially at the skull base rather than within the brainstem, the corticospinal and sensory tracts are spared, so there are no long-tract signs, and because it does not obstruct cerebrospinal fluid pathways there is characteristically no raised intracranial pressure or papilloedema. The result is a strikingly unilateral, progressive multiple cranial neuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and skull base with contrast to identify an infiltrative lesion
CT of the skull base to assess bony erosion of the foramina
Nasopharyngeal examination and biopsy where nasopharyngeal carcinoma is suspected
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including cytology for malignant or infective meningitis
Biopsy of any accessible skull-base lesion for histological diagnosis
Systemic imaging to identify a primary tumour or metastatic disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive unilateral multiple cranial nerve palsies indicating an aggressive skull-base process
Development of long-tract signs implying intra-axial extension
Bulbar involvement compromising swallowing and airway protection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely that of the underlying cause; when due to an infiltrative skull-base malignancy such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma the outlook is generally guarded, though early identification and directed treatment of the responsible lesion offer the best chance of stabilising the deficits.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the deficits as an intra-axial brainstem lesion and delaying skull-base imaging
Failing to examine the nasopharynx in a patient with progressive unilateral cranial neuropathies
Attributing progressive palsies to idiopathic causes without excluding malignancy
Overlooking cerebrospinal fluid cytology when carcinomatous meningitis is possible
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Direct treatment at the underlying skull-base pathology, most often chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma or an alternative regimen for lymphoma, metastasis or chordoma
Obtain a tissue diagnosis by nasopharyngeal or skull-base biopsy to guide oncological therapy
Give corticosteroids to reduce peritumoural oedema and compressive cranial neuropathy
Provide supportive rehabilitation for cranial-nerve deficits, including swallowing and speech therapy and corneal or eye protection for facial or trigeminal palsy
Manage neuropathic and cancer-related pain with appropriate analgesia
Coordinate care through a skull-base multidisciplinary team spanning ENT, neurology, and radiation and medical oncology
Involve palliative care where the underlying malignancy is advanced
